commenti.body:
Isn’t a plot really just the list of sequential events that make up a story? So I’d argue you can’t have a narrative without a plot.

But you can have a plot without much of a story.

There are lots of heavily plotted genre films, that barely have a story — because the narrative doesn’t invest us in any of the characters or the stakes. We don’t care what happens if a character faces challenges or changes. Or we get the sense that the filmmakers don’t really care either and the plot is an excuse to hang a set pieces and visual flourishes on.

It’s the deep investment of Scorsese and all his collaborators in every moment of the film that makes the story of “Goodfellas” compelling in spite of the fact that it’s not some sort of masterfully plotted conventional narrative or mainstream thriller.

By any definition of a plot, yes. It's absurd to argue that the film doesn't have a plot because in essence all a plot is, is the arrangement of story elements into an identifiable structure. The film is in no way "episodic", it linearly follows Henry Hill's life and even if it *were* episodic that wouldn't mean that it doesn't have a plot. Even much more abstract films or non-linear films still have plots. Whoever was arguing that it doesn't have a plot just doesn't understand what the term means.

Wait until they find out about anthologies. This is sort of an absurd claim for movie that is linear with clear cause and effect. The does not have a plot argument is just nonsense, Idk how anyone could watch a film and think this way lol

I personally feel that Goodfellas has a plot in that it has a clear beginning, middle and end. However, I think what you are identifying are the characteristics of a **picaresque** narrative which is episodic in nature and is one in which the main character does not change who they are. 

*Characteristics of picaresque narratives (as copy and pasted from Wikipedia):*

\- A picaresque narrative is usually written in first person as an autobiographical account.

\- The main character is often of low character or social class. They get by with wits and rarely deign to hold a job.

\- **There is little or no plot. The story is told in a series of loosely connected adventures or episodes.**

\- There is little if any character development in the main character. Once a pícaro, always a pícaro. Their circumstances may change but these rarely result in a change of heart.

\- The pícaro's story is told with a plainness of language or realism.

\- Satire is sometimes a prominent element. 

\- The behavior of a picaresque protagonist stops just short of criminality. Carefree or immoral rascality positions the picaresque hero as a sympathetic outsider, untouched by the false rules of society. 

I think one could make the point that Goodfellas is a clear picaresque narrative, and, as such, the narrative is more episodic in nature (particularly because Henry doesn't change). The circumstances for him change, but these are mostly the result of him getting involved with drugs. Obviously one clear divergence could be that a characteristic of the picaresque narrative is that the protagonist "stops just short of criminality", but you could make the argument that because (unlike Tommy and Jimmy) **Henry never actually kills anyone** directly, he also stops "just short of criminality". His crimes relate more to drug use and drug dealing, which many may argue is not truly criminal. 

That being said, I feel that Goodfellas does have a plot. Henry is born into a neighborhood in which the main "industry" is the mafia underworld. He joins this industry and rises through the ranks. However, he attempts to break from the group by getting involved with drugs - despite there being a clear prohibition against drug dealing or drug use. This decision separates him from the protection that the group provided and he has to fend for himself. In this sense, you could argue that it's a similar narrative as the Garden of Eden. The Forbidden Apple in this case is cocaine. Once he tastes the apple, everything falls apart and he is cast out into the "ordinary world" where he is "an average nobody".

Martin Scorsese famously said The Departed was the first movie he ever made that had a plot. I think that’s a bit of an exaggeration, but he believes in a distinction between plot and story. Plot driven narratives are one way to tell a story whereas he prefers character driven narratives. 

In the Departed, you have a cop undercover with the mob, and a mobster undercover with the police and each of them is tasked with finding out who the other side’s mole is. That’s plot. It being a Scorsese movie, also has great character driven moments, but the overriding story engine is the plot of them smoking each other out. 

In Goodfellas, you have Henry Hill, who Scorsese recently compared to Virgil, guiding Dante (us) through the underworld.  The story moves as Hill introduces us to new aspects of mob life, and to the characters who make up that life. There’s no through line of a task or goal that the characters are trying to achieve (plot) it’s strictly about the world and the people who inhabit it. Character driven. 

So in this sense, no. Goodfellas does not have plot. It’s a character driven story.
Responses so far I’ve been negative but I think you have a point OP.  It’s not one single story, it’s one self-contained story after another. I do feel like a plot is more than that.
